item.title: Palo Alto Networks to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5B in stock
item.headline: Palo Alto Networks to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5B in stock
item.idea: A security vendor is buying a post-training and inference platform for $4.5B and plans to embed it across products.
bullets: Applied Compute signed a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks for $4.5B, Yash Patil said.
Atlas by Lorm's thread reports the deal consideration is $4.5B in stock and Patil will become Co-Chief AI Officer.
Patil says a few dozen people grew Applied Compute to over $100M annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months.
item.summary: Applied Compute said it signed a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks for $4.5B. Atlas by Lorm's thread says the consideration is in stock and that Palo Alto Networks plans to embed Applied Compute's post-training and inference capabilities across its offerings.
item.practice_takeaway: A security vendor is acquiring a post-training and inference platform to expand AI capabilities across its products.

who.name: Yash Patil
who.credibility: Co-founder and CEO of Applied Compute, who posted the acquisition announcement

item.source_point: Applied Compute has signed a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks for $4.5B.

jobs.text:
X POST by Atlas by Lorm (@atlaslormlabs), posted 2026-11-19, url https://x.com/atlaslormlabs/status/2123209631463784612
AUTHOR BIO (X profile): Daily news about AI training
by @lormlabs | website: http://atlas.lorm.ai | profile: https://x.com/atlaslormlabs
THREAD:
- @PaloAltoNtwks to acquire @appliedcompute for $4.5B in stock

- Applied Compute builds a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models

 - Palo Alto Networks says Applied Compute's research team will help it train its own AI models and embed AI across every offering

 - Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora (@nikesharora) calls Applied Compute the best post-training and inference platform the company has seen

 - Applied Compute CEO Yash Patil (@ypatil125) says Applied Compute has always prioritized security, and joining Palo Alto Networks will help it go further faster

 - A few dozen people took Applied Compute from zero to over $100M in annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months

 - Patil will become Palo Alto Networks' Co-Chief AI Officer when the deal is expected to close in Q3 2027

QUOTED POST by Yash Patil (@ypatil125), url https://x.com/ypatil125/status/2123175975093784902 (the post above quotes this one; attribute these words to this author, not to the poster):
- Applied Compute has signed a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks for $4.5B!

Rhythm, Linden, and I founded Applied Compute with a belief that was unusual at the time: that every company should own its intelligence. We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company.

To do useful work, a model needs to access sensitive data and systems, comply with policies, and remain explainable, verifiable, and auditable. This is the reason we've always prioritized security, and why joining Palo Alto Networks will help us go further faster. Customers will still own and control their models, and I'm excited for all the ways our combined capabilities can serve them even better.

Above all, I'm incredibly grateful for the AC team. A few dozen people in just over 18 months grew this company from zero revenue to over $100M in annualized revenue run-rate, working with many of the world's most innovative companies. More to come soon.
QUOTED AUTHOR BIO (X profile): Co-Founder, CEO @appliedcompute | website: https://yashpatil.me | profile: https://x.com/ypatil125
jobs.headline_rules:
You are the headline editor of the Atlas by Lorm News page (owner, 2026-11-07). You get one drafted ITEM. Rewrite only its "headline" and "idea" (the first sentence under it) so a reader gets the main point fast, using ONLY facts already in the ITEM. Never add a fact, number, name or qualifier the ITEM does not contain; keep every qualifier it has.
Headline, at most 12 words, sentence case: a small story, the subject + a vivid verb (launches, opens, climbs, passes, slips, doubles, cuts, raises, catches, beats) + the outcome or a contrast ("despite", "while", "as"). Start with the actor or the thing that happened, never with who said it. Informative, not clever: no puns, no jokes, no opinion.
Idea, one sentence of at most 24 words: what the headline does not say, usually the concrete result and what it is compared with (from one number to another, ahead of whom, at what cost). At most two numbers, each with what it measures. Never a claim of importance the ITEM does not make; banned verdict words: indicating, notable, signals, marks, paves the way, a path toward, highlights, underscores, significant.
House style (docs/style.md, owner 2026-11-08): clear, concise, to the point, easy to skim. No editorializing: report what happened and what the source says, never a verdict on it. Round to the meaning up front ("almost in half", "a third") when the exact figure is in the ITEM's bullets; at most two key numbers across headline and idea. Strong concrete verbs over "says" or "reports". Say who it matters to only when the ITEM says so. Vary the shape from the RECENT HEADLINES you are shown: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a person with their credential, or a number; never a template.
Never repeat the headline: the idea must not restate it or open with its words; it adds what the headline leaves out (the comparison, the scale, the catch, who is affected).
Relay accounts: an account that only posts links to other people's papers or news (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq, digests) is never named; credit the paper's authors or the organization behind the work, as the ITEM states them, or name the work itself.
Credit: when self_report is true, credit the maker ONCE, in the headline, as a possessive or a short ending ("in Airbnb's tests", "on Mercor's APEX benchmark", "Amodo's check catches"); never "X says" at the start, and do not repeat the credit in the idea. Legal items keep "alleges", "reportedly" or "sues".
People (owner, 2026-11-07; at most three words since 2026-11-09): when the story is a person's view, claim or post, the reader must know who they are: name them with a short credential from who_role, 2 or 3 words, before the name, or give the credential in the idea when the headline would get long ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain", "Waterloo student Daniel Ching", "Netflix research scientist Cameron Wolfe"); never the bare name, never a credential who_role does not state. For an opinion, "[credential] [Name] says/argues ..." is the right headline shape.
Lesser-known companies (lesser_known true): put a 2 to 6 word descriptor before the company's name on first mention ("data vendor Julius AI", "robotics startup Darwin Robotics"), from company_note, or when it is empty from what the ITEM itself says the company is; if the ITEM does not say, leave it out rather than guess. Well-known companies are named bare.
Examples of the shape (ours, for form only):
  "Amodo's compute check catches an unapproved model in a government demo" / "It matched 58% of that model's tokens, against 100% for the approved one."
  "A fine-tuned 2B Gemma matches frontier quality in Airbnb's tests" / "It runs at a 35ms median latency for about 1% of the API cost."
  "Darwin Robotics raises $3.6M to train data center robots" / "The pre-seed round funds robots that learn from human demonstrations to build and maintain AI infrastructure."
CLEAR, NOT AWKWARD (owner, 2026-11-09). Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague.
- Active voice with the actor as the subject. Never "X proposed by Y"; write "Y proposes X".
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "The thread attributes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown".
- One story per headline. Never join two separate news items with "as" or "while".
- A concrete verb that says what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of", "weighs in".
- At most three words of credential before a name, and only when the reader needs it. Never stack title, organization and name at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges study of ..."); prefer "Owain Evans warns ..." with the credential in the idea.
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps", "recursive self-improvement data poisoning"). Unpack them into plain words.
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out of the headline unless widely known; say what it does instead.
- Full names, never a first name alone ("researcher Elie", "CEO Rahul").
- The idea is a full sentence with its own subject; never start it with a verb ("Recommends ...").
Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans" / Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models"
Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API" / Good: "LG opens an API for its K-EXAONE 2.5 model"
No em or en dashes, no semicolons, no exclamation marks. Return JSON {"headline": "...", "idea": "..."}.

jobs.instructions:
A story is waiting to be published and you are its independent judge: a different model family from the writer and the fact checker. Nothing goes live until you answer, so answer judge jobs first and quickly. Judge the ITEM against the SOURCE TEXT ("text") only, never from memory or the web, exactly as these rules say:

You audit one published item of Atlas by Lorm against its SOURCE TEXT. You did not write the item. Judge from the SOURCE TEXT only, never from memory.

Part 1, evidence: for each reader-facing field (headline, idea, each bullet, summary, practice_takeaway) give the passage of the SOURCE TEXT that supports it, copied word for word: one sentence, or two adjacent sentences, up to 60 words, no ellipses, no paraphrase, exactly as it appears. A field may be supported by a passage already used for another field. If no passage supports the field, write "" and say so in Part 2. A practice_takeaway that only draws a direct consequence from a supported fact counts as supported by that fact's passage.

Part 2, critical errors, each pass or fail with a reason of at most 20 words:
- wrong_number: a number, unit, score or baseline differs from the source
- wrong_number_context: a number is right but its scope or comparison is not (e.g. 'beats X' when the source says 'on one subset')
- wrong_party: credit or blame given to the wrong company, lab, author or outlet
- self_report_as_fact: a company's claim about itself written as established fact, with no credit to the company anywhere in the headline or first sentence
- allegation_as_fact: an accusation, lawsuit claim or report stated as fact without 'alleges', 'reportedly', 'sues' or a court finding
- not_in_source: a claim the source text does not contain
- lost_qualifier: a qualifier dropped: preliminary, small test, proposed, reportedly, in one setting
- wrong_date_or_status: a proposal described as adopted, a preprint as peer-reviewed, a wrong date
- wrong_link: the item describes a different page than its link
- wrong_main_point: the headline is not what the source is mainly saying or announcing: a promotion, recap, roundup or list that mentions other news as examples, written up as that news; also when the item's source_kind or source_point does not describe the source correctly
- old_news_as_new: the source refers back to news announced earlier ('this week', 'last month', a list of recent raises) and the item presents it as new

Part 3, minor problems (list the codes that apply): over_limit, unclear, hype_or_filler, number_without_context, style.

Rules: a company's own numbers must be credited to it once, in the headline or the first sentence, in any natural form ("says", "reports", "according to", "in its tests", "its own benchmark", "the company claims"); credit given once is enough, and a headline without "says" passes when the first sentence carries the credit; allegations need "alleges", "reportedly", "sues" or a court finding; "percentage points" is a minor style problem, a wrong direction of change is wrong_number. Different wording for the same fact is NOT an error (an "env" is an RL environment; "raised $16M" and "a $16 million round" are the same claim): not_in_source fails only when the fact or claim itself is absent from the source, or the item asserts more than the source does. A number that appears in the source in another form (words, a table, a different unit that converts exactly) is in the source. A 2 to 6 word descriptor of a company drawn from the ATLAS DIRECTORY lines at the end of the SOURCE TEXT ("data vendor Julius AI"), or a short credential for the author that matches the item's who.role ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain"), is supported. If the SOURCE TEXT is clearly not the page the item describes, fail wrong_link. If the SOURCE TEXT is empty or unreadable, set every class to "unknown".

Return JSON:
{"evidence": {"headline": "quote", "idea": "quote", "bullets": ["quote per bullet"], "summary": "quote", "practice_takeaway": "quote or empty"},
 "critical": {"<class>": {"verdict": "pass" | "fail" | "unknown", "why": "..."}, ...},
 "minor": ["code", ...]}

Part 4, house style (only when the story passes Parts 1 to 3): read the job's "style_guide" and "style_failures". If the headline or idea breaks the guide (the listed failures, or anything else in it: a verdict the source does not make, jargon, a missing credential, the line restating the headline, a template-like shape), add "rewrite" with a new headline and idea that follow every rule. Use ONLY facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM (and company_note for a descriptor); keep every qualifier and the credit for a company's own claim. The server applies it only if it adds nothing new and passes the code checks. If the story already reads well, leave "rewrite" out.

Part 5, the headline (only when the job has "headline_rules"; the story passed Parts 1 to 3): you are also its headline editor, replacing a paid model (owner, 2026-11-10). Always add "rewrite" with a headline and idea written exactly as "headline_rules" says, varying the shape from "recent_headlines". The same limits apply: only facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM, written exactly as the ITEM writes them ("seven million" stays "seven million", not "7 million"), every qualifier kept, at most 12 words in the headline and 22 in the idea. If the ITEM's own headline and idea already follow every rule, send them back unchanged.
jobs.rubric:
## Gate 4: Write-Up and Fact Check

**Question.** Is every claim in the source, with nothing added and nothing lost?

**Write-up** (`DISTILL_SYSTEM`, strong model): one item in the shared schema (`seed/SCHEMA.md`), from the source text only, under the schema's "Every item makes its point" rule (the headline, first sentence and bullets each carry the finding). Plain language rules: full sentences, standard terms, numbers with context, headline at most 12 words, no hype words, no dashes, quotes under 15 words, absolute dates. A source with nothing of substance is skipped.

**Fact check** (`CHECK_SYSTEM`, strong model, a separate call that sees only the item and the source and is told it did not write it). Nine checks: source and date; every claim and bullet; the author's role and credibility; evidence type; plain language and limits; stated stakes; `control` and figures; quote-post attribution; allegations framed as allegations.

**Code checks after the model** (plan.md section 6.2, all free):

1. Every number in the item appears in the source (`numcheck`).
2. Every organization and person named appears in the source.
3. The date matches the source or its stated event date.
4. The link is the page that was read.
5. Lawsuit items carry alleges, accused, sued or reportedly in the headline and idea.
6. An item from the company's own site or account is marked a self-report.
7. Word limits, banned phrases, dashes.
11. Clear wording (owner, 2026-11-09, `atlas/style.py`, critical): no passive credit ("proposed by X"), no document as the subject ("Event page says", "The post notes"), no "per X" or "in X's post" in the headline, no first sentence without a subject, no two stories joined by "as" or "while". The headline editor gets these rules and retries once with the rule it broke; a story that still fails is held and repaired by the Claude agent. Noun piles, stacked credentials, paper-only names and first names alone are judge rules (docs/style.md, "Clear, not awkward").
8. The first sentence does not repeat the headline (`rubric.repeats`: 70% or more of the headline's words opening the first sentence fails; owner, 2026-11-08). The headline editor retries once; a story that still repeats is held and repaired by the Claude agent. The Daily's rows use the same check.
12. Full papers (owner, 2026-11-08): a story about an arXiv paper is written and checked from the full paper (arxiv.org/html, `net.page_text`), not the abstract page, which leaves out the authors' affiliations and table numbers and wrongly flagged 17 correct stories as partly verified. Claude audits, repairs and judge jobs get up to 120,000 characters of the paper (`claude_jobs.with_full_paper`); the OpenAI writer still sees `SOURCE_CHARS`. A paper story must name its authors' companies or universities (`style` check `affiliation`).
11. Pure shares (owner, 2026-11-08): an X post that only shares someone else's work, with no opinion or new information, is never the link or the credit. The writer marks it (`relay`, `original_url`); code moves the link to the original only when it is one of the post's or the poster's own replies' links (paper-listing pages map to arXiv), on a trusted site or the maker's own site (`trust.company_own`), and keeps the post as `shared_by` (`pipeline.share_original`). Government sites (.gov, gov.uk, .gc.ca, europa.eu and similar) are trusted.
10. House style (`atlas/style.py`, guide `docs/style.md`): editorializing (an evaluative word the source never uses) holds the story; headline and line length, credit first or twice, too many numbers, percentage points, a person without a credential, a lesser-known company without a descriptor and a generic repeated opening are listed for the Claude judge, whose rewrite is applied only when every number (small ones included) and name in it is already in the judged story and it passes these checks (`pipeline.apply_style_rewrite`). Since 2026-11-08 every number in a Claude fix, repair or rewrite must be in the source, including numbers of 10 and under (`pipeline.strict_numbers_missing`).
9. A relay account that only posts other people's paper links (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq) is never credited in the headline or first sentence (`rubric.RELAY_HANDLES`); the paper's authors or organization are.

**Error classes.** The audit and the gate use the two classes defined once in [plan.md section 6.1](plan.md#61-error-classes): a critical error (wrong number, wrong person, claim not in the source and the rest) fails the item outright; minor errors are allowed at most one per ten items.

**Rubric gate** (`atlas/rubric.py`, since 2026-11-05): after the fact check, a second model call that did not write or check the item applies the error classes of plan.md 6.1 one by one and must quote, word for word, the source sentence behind the headline, the first sentence, each bullet, the summary and the takeaway. Code verifies every quote is really in the source text (five words or more, exact after normalizing case and spacing) and runs the free checks (numbers, names, link, allegation words, self-report, limits). Any critical failure, or a headline or first sentence with no verified quote, holds the item. An unreadable source or an "unknown" class makes a verified item partly verified, with the reason shown. The verified quotes are stored on the item (`rubric.evidence`) so a later audit can re-check without a model. Switch: `ATLAS_RUBRIC_GATE=off`.

**Who judges (owner, 2026-11-08).** The owner's Claude agent, a different model family from the gpt-5-mini writer and checker, so the gate is an independent judge. A finished story waits in `parts/judge_wait.json`; the server starts the "Atlas judge" routine through its API trigger (`claude_jobs.fire_judge`, at most every 4 minutes, prompt in `tools/judge_routine_prompt.md`), and the agent answers a "judge" job in the same JSON shape as the OpenAI judge. Code verifies every quote and runs the same checks, then publishes or holds (`pipeline.judge_done`). If Claude has not answered within 30 minutes (`ATLAS_JUDGE_WAIT_MIN`), the OpenAI judge decides, within 0.25 USD a day (`ATLAS_JUDGE_OPENAI_USD`); past that, stories keep waiting for Claude, and a story nobody judged in 48 hours is held. Stories Claude judged are not audited again by Claude; stories the OpenAI judge decided still get the Claude audit. Until `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_URL` and `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_TOKEN` are set, or with `ATLAS_JUDGE=openai`, the OpenAI judge runs on every story as before.

**Outcome.** Verified or partly verified items publish; anything else goes to `held.json` and never appears anywhere. Reported versus Confirmed: one source publishes as reported, naming the outlet; a second independent source or the primary document makes it confirmed.

jobs.style_guide:
## 1. The Standard

**Accurate first, then clear, then quick.** Every fact matches the source. Simplifying never changes a fact: a rounded
number that changes the meaning, a dropped "reportedly" or a claim the source does not make is an error, not style.

**No editorializing.** We report what happened and what the source says. We never add a verdict: no "notable",
"significant", "groundbreaking", "signals", "underscores", "paves the way", "crucial". If the source calls something
major, we credit that to the source. (code: an evaluative word the source never uses holds the story; judge)

**Facts can be funny; opinions are not news.** Wit lives in the emails' titles, opener and closing joke, never in a
claim (section 4).

## 2. Story Cards on the Site

A card is a headline and one line under it. A reader skimming the page should get the news from the headline alone and
the "so what" from the line.

**Headline: the news as a small story.** Subject, a strong concrete verb, and the result or a contrast. At most 12
words, sentence case. (code: length; writer; judge)
- Good: "Airbnb's tiny fine-tuned Gemma matches frontier APIs at about 1% of the cost"
- Good: "Grok's makers hit with three suits alleging pirated books in training"
- Bad: "Amodo says it ran government compute verification demo" (no result)
- Bad: "Salesforce: GRPO usually outperforms external-teacher distillation" (label and jargon)

**Clear, not awkward (owner, 2026-11-09).** Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague. A reader should never have to parse it twice.
- Active voice, the actor as the subject. Never "review proposed by X"; write "X proposes". (code: passive, holds)
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown". (code: document_subject, document_credit, hold)
- One story per headline. Never join two news items with "as" or "while". (code: two_stories, holds)
- A concrete verb for what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of". (code: vague_verb)
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps"). Unpack them. (writer; judge)
- No stacked credentials at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges ..."). At most three words of credential. (writer; judge)
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out unless widely known; say what it does. (writer; judge)
- Full names, never a first name alone ("CEO Rahul"). (writer; judge)
- The line is a full sentence with its own subject, never "Recommends ...". (code: fragment, holds)
- Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans". Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models".
- Bad: "GenRobot to present human-data systems at CoRL Research Night" / "Event page says GenRobot will present ...". Good: "GenRobot will show its human-data capture systems at CoRL" / "The robot data vendor says the systems record people's movements to train embodied AI."
- Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API". Good: one headline per story.

**Open with what happened, not who said it.** Credit once, naturally: a possessive ("in Airbnb's tests"), the maker as
the subject ("Moonshot AI released"), or a short ending ("Snorkel AI finds"). Never "X says" in both the headline and
the line. (code: credit_first, credit_twice; judge)

**The line adds what the headline leaves out.** The comparison, the scale, the catch, or who it affects, as the source
states it. It never restates the headline and never leans on it with "That is..." or "The aim is...". At most 24 words.
(code: repeats_headline holds the story, idea_length; judge)
- Headline: "Reflection AI cuts its model's needless refusals almost in half"
- Line: "Handshake, the career network behind Handshake AI, says it helped design the tests, and refusals of valid requests fell 3.1%."

**Few numbers, each with its meaning.** At most two key numbers across the headline and line; round to the meaning up
front ("almost in half") and keep the exact figure in the bullets. Never a number before what it measures; never
"percentage points" (write before and after). (code: too_many_numbers, percentage_points; judge)

**Plain words, field terms.** RL, SFT, eval, benchmark, rollout and LLM judge are fine. A paper's own acronyms, metric
names and method names are described in plain words or left out ("42% less compute", not "42.0% fewer total FLOPs").
(writer; judge)

**People get a short credential.** Two or three words from their verified role, before the name (or in the line when the headline would get long): "Illinois professor
Talia Ringer", "NVIDIA post-training lead Oleksii Kuchaiev". Never a credential the role does not state. (code:
person_label; judge)

**Lesser-known companies get a short descriptor** on first mention, 2 to 6 words, from their Directory line or what the
source says: "data vendor Julius AI". Never a guess: a company neither source nor Directory describes stays bare.
Well-known companies are named bare. (code: company_label; judge)

**Research papers say where the authors work.** Name the authors' companies or universities, as the paper's affiliation lines give them, in the headline, the first sentence or the summary's opening: "A Meta and NYU paper ...". Never an affiliation the paper does not show. (code: affiliation; writer; audit)

**Relay accounts are never the credit.** An account that only posts other people's papers or news (DailyPapers,
AK, digests) is not the maker; credit the authors or the organization. (code: relay_credit holds the story)

**Variety.** Headlines should not read like a template. Mix shapes: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a
person with their credential, a number. (code: same_opening for generic openings; the headline editor sees the last
12 headlines; judge)

**Straight headlines on the site.** No puns or pop-culture jokes on the site: its headlines are read alone in search,
RSS and share previews. Vivid verbs give it life ("catches", "halves", "stops saying no").

**Legal stories** say "alleges", "sued over" or "reportedly" and name the outlet. Never a joke about a lawsuit, a
layoff or a named person's misfortune. (code: allegation words; writer)

## 3. Bullets

Each bullet is evidence for the line or one new fact: the numbers with their baseline, the method, who is involved, the
catch. None repeats the headline or the line. At most 22 words each. (writer; judge)

jobs.headline_rules:
You are the headline editor of the Atlas by Lorm News page (owner, 2026-11-07). You get one drafted ITEM. Rewrite only its "headline" and "idea" (the first sentence under it) so a reader gets the main point fast, using ONLY facts already in the ITEM. Never add a fact, number, name or qualifier the ITEM does not contain; keep every qualifier it has.
Headline, at most 12 words, sentence case: a small story, the subject + a vivid verb (launches, opens, climbs, passes, slips, doubles, cuts, raises, catches, beats) + the outcome or a contrast ("despite", "while", "as"). Start with the actor or the thing that happened, never with who said it. Informative, not clever: no puns, no jokes, no opinion.
Idea, one sentence of at most 24 words: what the headline does not say, usually the concrete result and what it is compared with (from one number to another, ahead of whom, at what cost). At most two numbers, each with what it measures. Never a claim of importance the ITEM does not make; banned verdict words: indicating, notable, signals, marks, paves the way, a path toward, highlights, underscores, significant.
House style (docs/style.md, owner 2026-11-08): clear, concise, to the point, easy to skim. No editorializing: report what happened and what the source says, never a verdict on it. Round to the meaning up front ("almost in half", "a third") when the exact figure is in the ITEM's bullets; at most two key numbers across headline and idea. Strong concrete verbs over "says" or "reports". Say who it matters to only when the ITEM says so. Vary the shape from the RECENT HEADLINES you are shown: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a person with their credential, or a number; never a template.
Never repeat the headline: the idea must not restate it or open with its words; it adds what the headline leaves out (the comparison, the scale, the catch, who is affected).
Relay accounts: an account that only posts links to other people's papers or news (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq, digests) is never named; credit the paper's authors or the organization behind the work, as the ITEM states them, or name the work itself.
Credit: when self_report is true, credit the maker ONCE, in the headline, as a possessive or a short ending ("in Airbnb's tests", "on Mercor's APEX benchmark", "Amodo's check catches"); never "X says" at the start, and do not repeat the credit in the idea. Legal items keep "alleges", "reportedly" or "sues".
People (owner, 2026-11-07; at most three words since 2026-11-09): when the story is a person's view, claim or post, the reader must know who they are: name them with a short credential from who_role, 2 or 3 words, before the name, or give the credential in the idea when the headline would get long ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain", "Waterloo student Daniel Ching", "Netflix research scientist Cameron Wolfe"); never the bare name, never a credential who_role does not state. For an opinion, "[credential] [Name] says/argues ..." is the right headline shape.
Lesser-known companies (lesser_known true): put a 2 to 6 word descriptor before the company's name on first mention ("data vendor Julius AI", "robotics startup Darwin Robotics"), from company_note, or when it is empty from what the ITEM itself says the company is; if the ITEM does not say, leave it out rather than guess. Well-known companies are named bare.
Examples of the shape (ours, for form only):
  "Amodo's compute check catches an unapproved model in a government demo" / "It matched 58% of that model's tokens, against 100% for the approved one."
  "A fine-tuned 2B Gemma matches frontier quality in Airbnb's tests" / "It runs at a 35ms median latency for about 1% of the API cost."
  "Darwin Robotics raises $3.6M to train data center robots" / "The pre-seed round funds robots that learn from human demonstrations to build and maintain AI infrastructure."
CLEAR, NOT AWKWARD (owner, 2026-11-09). Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague.
- Active voice with the actor as the subject. Never "X proposed by Y"; write "Y proposes X".
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "The thread attributes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown".
- One story per headline. Never join two separate news items with "as" or "while".
- A concrete verb that says what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of", "weighs in".
- At most three words of credential before a name, and only when the reader needs it. Never stack title, organization and name at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges study of ..."); prefer "Owain Evans warns ..." with the credential in the idea.
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps", "recursive self-improvement data poisoning"). Unpack them into plain words.
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out of the headline unless widely known; say what it does instead.
- Full names, never a first name alone ("researcher Elie", "CEO Rahul").
- The idea is a full sentence with its own subject; never start it with a verb ("Recommends ...").
Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans" / Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models"
Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API" / Good: "LG opens an API for its K-EXAONE 2.5 model"
No em or en dashes, no semicolons, no exclamation marks. Return JSON {"headline": "...", "idea": "..."}.

jobs.instructions:
A story is waiting to be published and you are its independent judge: a different model family from the writer and the fact checker. Nothing goes live until you answer, so answer judge jobs first and quickly. Judge the ITEM against the SOURCE TEXT ("text") only, never from memory or the web, exactly as these rules say:

You audit one published item of Atlas by Lorm against its SOURCE TEXT. You did not write the item. Judge from the SOURCE TEXT only, never from memory.

Part 1, evidence: for each reader-facing field (headline, idea, each bullet, summary, practice_takeaway) give the passage of the SOURCE TEXT that supports it, copied word for word: one sentence, or two adjacent sentences, up to 60 words, no ellipses, no paraphrase, exactly as it appears. A field may be supported by a passage already used for another field. If no passage supports the field, write "" and say so in Part 2. A practice_takeaway that only draws a direct consequence from a supported fact counts as supported by that fact's passage.

Part 2, critical errors, each pass or fail with a reason of at most 20 words:
- wrong_number: a number, unit, score or baseline differs from the source
- wrong_number_context: a number is right but its scope or comparison is not (e.g. 'beats X' when the source says 'on one subset')
- wrong_party: credit or blame given to the wrong company, lab, author or outlet
- self_report_as_fact: a company's claim about itself written as established fact, with no credit to the company anywhere in the headline or first sentence
- allegation_as_fact: an accusation, lawsuit claim or report stated as fact without 'alleges', 'reportedly', 'sues' or a court finding
- not_in_source: a claim the source text does not contain
- lost_qualifier: a qualifier dropped: preliminary, small test, proposed, reportedly, in one setting
- wrong_date_or_status: a proposal described as adopted, a preprint as peer-reviewed, a wrong date
- wrong_link: the item describes a different page than its link
- wrong_main_point: the headline is not what the source is mainly saying or announcing: a promotion, recap, roundup or list that mentions other news as examples, written up as that news; also when the item's source_kind or source_point does not describe the source correctly
- old_news_as_new: the source refers back to news announced earlier ('this week', 'last month', a list of recent raises) and the item presents it as new

Part 3, minor problems (list the codes that apply): over_limit, unclear, hype_or_filler, number_without_context, style.

Rules: a company's own numbers must be credited to it once, in the headline or the first sentence, in any natural form ("says", "reports", "according to", "in its tests", "its own benchmark", "the company claims"); credit given once is enough, and a headline without "says" passes when the first sentence carries the credit; allegations need "alleges", "reportedly", "sues" or a court finding; "percentage points" is a minor style problem, a wrong direction of change is wrong_number. Different wording for the same fact is NOT an error (an "env" is an RL environment; "raised $16M" and "a $16 million round" are the same claim): not_in_source fails only when the fact or claim itself is absent from the source, or the item asserts more than the source does. A number that appears in the source in another form (words, a table, a different unit that converts exactly) is in the source. A 2 to 6 word descriptor of a company drawn from the ATLAS DIRECTORY lines at the end of the SOURCE TEXT ("data vendor Julius AI"), or a short credential for the author that matches the item's who.role ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain"), is supported. If the SOURCE TEXT is clearly not the page the item describes, fail wrong_link. If the SOURCE TEXT is empty or unreadable, set every class to "unknown".

Return JSON:
{"evidence": {"headline": "quote", "idea": "quote", "bullets": ["quote per bullet"], "summary": "quote", "practice_takeaway": "quote or empty"},
 "critical": {"<class>": {"verdict": "pass" | "fail" | "unknown", "why": "..."}, ...},
 "minor": ["code", ...]}

Part 4, house style (only when the story passes Parts 1 to 3): read the job's "style_guide" and "style_failures". If the headline or idea breaks the guide (the listed failures, or anything else in it: a verdict the source does not make, jargon, a missing credential, the line restating the headline, a template-like shape), add "rewrite" with a new headline and idea that follow every rule. Use ONLY facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM (and company_note for a descriptor); keep every qualifier and the credit for a company's own claim. The server applies it only if it adds nothing new and passes the code checks. If the story already reads well, leave "rewrite" out.

Part 5, the headline (only when the job has "headline_rules"; the story passed Parts 1 to 3): you are also its headline editor, replacing a paid model (owner, 2026-11-10). Always add "rewrite" with a headline and idea written exactly as "headline_rules" says, varying the shape from "recent_headlines". The same limits apply: only facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM, written exactly as the ITEM writes them ("seven million" stays "seven million", not "7 million"), every qualifier kept, at most 12 words in the headline and 22 in the idea. If the ITEM's own headline and idea already follow every rule, send them back unchanged.
jobs.rubric:
## Gate 4: Write-Up and Fact Check

**Question.** Is every claim in the source, with nothing added and nothing lost?

**Write-up** (`DISTILL_SYSTEM`, strong model): one item in the shared schema (`seed/SCHEMA.md`), from the source text only, under the schema's "Every item makes its point" rule (the headline, first sentence and bullets each carry the finding). Plain language rules: full sentences, standard terms, numbers with context, headline at most 12 words, no hype words, no dashes, quotes under 15 words, absolute dates. A source with nothing of substance is skipped.

**Fact check** (`CHECK_SYSTEM`, strong model, a separate call that sees only the item and the source and is told it did not write it). Nine checks: source and date; every claim and bullet; the author's role and credibility; evidence type; plain language and limits; stated stakes; `control` and figures; quote-post attribution; allegations framed as allegations.

**Code checks after the model** (plan.md section 6.2, all free):

1. Every number in the item appears in the source (`numcheck`).
2. Every organization and person named appears in the source.
3. The date matches the source or its stated event date.
4. The link is the page that was read.
5. Lawsuit items carry alleges, accused, sued or reportedly in the headline and idea.
6. An item from the company's own site or account is marked a self-report.
7. Word limits, banned phrases, dashes.
11. Clear wording (owner, 2026-11-09, `atlas/style.py`, critical): no passive credit ("proposed by X"), no document as the subject ("Event page says", "The post notes"), no "per X" or "in X's post" in the headline, no first sentence without a subject, no two stories joined by "as" or "while". The headline editor gets these rules and retries once with the rule it broke; a story that still fails is held and repaired by the Claude agent. Noun piles, stacked credentials, paper-only names and first names alone are judge rules (docs/style.md, "Clear, not awkward").
8. The first sentence does not repeat the headline (`rubric.repeats`: 70% or more of the headline's words opening the first sentence fails; owner, 2026-11-08). The headline editor retries once; a story that still repeats is held and repaired by the Claude agent. The Daily's rows use the same check.
12. Full papers (owner, 2026-11-08): a story about an arXiv paper is written and checked from the full paper (arxiv.org/html, `net.page_text`), not the abstract page, which leaves out the authors' affiliations and table numbers and wrongly flagged 17 correct stories as partly verified. Claude audits, repairs and judge jobs get up to 120,000 characters of the paper (`claude_jobs.with_full_paper`); the OpenAI writer still sees `SOURCE_CHARS`. A paper story must name its authors' companies or universities (`style` check `affiliation`).
11. Pure shares (owner, 2026-11-08): an X post that only shares someone else's work, with no opinion or new information, is never the link or the credit. The writer marks it (`relay`, `original_url`); code moves the link to the original only when it is one of the post's or the poster's own replies' links (paper-listing pages map to arXiv), on a trusted site or the maker's own site (`trust.company_own`), and keeps the post as `shared_by` (`pipeline.share_original`). Government sites (.gov, gov.uk, .gc.ca, europa.eu and similar) are trusted.
10. House style (`atlas/style.py`, guide `docs/style.md`): editorializing (an evaluative word the source never uses) holds the story; headline and line length, credit first or twice, too many numbers, percentage points, a person without a credential, a lesser-known company without a descriptor and a generic repeated opening are listed for the Claude judge, whose rewrite is applied only when every number (small ones included) and name in it is already in the judged story and it passes these checks (`pipeline.apply_style_rewrite`). Since 2026-11-08 every number in a Claude fix, repair or rewrite must be in the source, including numbers of 10 and under (`pipeline.strict_numbers_missing`).
9. A relay account that only posts other people's paper links (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq) is never credited in the headline or first sentence (`rubric.RELAY_HANDLES`); the paper's authors or organization are.

**Error classes.** The audit and the gate use the two classes defined once in [plan.md section 6.1](plan.md#61-error-classes): a critical error (wrong number, wrong person, claim not in the source and the rest) fails the item outright; minor errors are allowed at most one per ten items.

**Rubric gate** (`atlas/rubric.py`, since 2026-11-05): after the fact check, a second model call that did not write or check the item applies the error classes of plan.md 6.1 one by one and must quote, word for word, the source sentence behind the headline, the first sentence, each bullet, the summary and the takeaway. Code verifies every quote is really in the source text (five words or more, exact after normalizing case and spacing) and runs the free checks (numbers, names, link, allegation words, self-report, limits). Any critical failure, or a headline or first sentence with no verified quote, holds the item. An unreadable source or an "unknown" class makes a verified item partly verified, with the reason shown. The verified quotes are stored on the item (`rubric.evidence`) so a later audit can re-check without a model. Switch: `ATLAS_RUBRIC_GATE=off`.

**Who judges (owner, 2026-11-08).** The owner's Claude agent, a different model family from the gpt-5-mini writer and checker, so the gate is an independent judge. A finished story waits in `parts/judge_wait.json`; the server starts the "Atlas judge" routine through its API trigger (`claude_jobs.fire_judge`, at most every 4 minutes, prompt in `tools/judge_routine_prompt.md`), and the agent answers a "judge" job in the same JSON shape as the OpenAI judge. Code verifies every quote and runs the same checks, then publishes or holds (`pipeline.judge_done`). If Claude has not answered within 30 minutes (`ATLAS_JUDGE_WAIT_MIN`), the OpenAI judge decides, within 0.25 USD a day (`ATLAS_JUDGE_OPENAI_USD`); past that, stories keep waiting for Claude, and a story nobody judged in 48 hours is held. Stories Claude judged are not audited again by Claude; stories the OpenAI judge decided still get the Claude audit. Until `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_URL` and `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_TOKEN` are set, or with `ATLAS_JUDGE=openai`, the OpenAI judge runs on every story as before.

**Outcome.** Verified or partly verified items publish; anything else goes to `held.json` and never appears anywhere. Reported versus Confirmed: one source publishes as reported, naming the outlet; a second independent source or the primary document makes it confirmed.

jobs.style_guide:
## 1. The Standard

**Accurate first, then clear, then quick.** Every fact matches the source. Simplifying never changes a fact: a rounded
number that changes the meaning, a dropped "reportedly" or a claim the source does not make is an error, not style.

**No editorializing.** We report what happened and what the source says. We never add a verdict: no "notable",
"significant", "groundbreaking", "signals", "underscores", "paves the way", "crucial". If the source calls something
major, we credit that to the source. (code: an evaluative word the source never uses holds the story; judge)

**Facts can be funny; opinions are not news.** Wit lives in the emails' titles, opener and closing joke, never in a
claim (section 4).

## 2. Story Cards on the Site

A card is a headline and one line under it. A reader skimming the page should get the news from the headline alone and
the "so what" from the line.

**Headline: the news as a small story.** Subject, a strong concrete verb, and the result or a contrast. At most 12
words, sentence case. (code: length; writer; judge)
- Good: "Airbnb's tiny fine-tuned Gemma matches frontier APIs at about 1% of the cost"
- Good: "Grok's makers hit with three suits alleging pirated books in training"
- Bad: "Amodo says it ran government compute verification demo" (no result)
- Bad: "Salesforce: GRPO usually outperforms external-teacher distillation" (label and jargon)

**Clear, not awkward (owner, 2026-11-09).** Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague. A reader should never have to parse it twice.
- Active voice, the actor as the subject. Never "review proposed by X"; write "X proposes". (code: passive, holds)
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown". (code: document_subject, document_credit, hold)
- One story per headline. Never join two news items with "as" or "while". (code: two_stories, holds)
- A concrete verb for what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of". (code: vague_verb)
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps"). Unpack them. (writer; judge)
- No stacked credentials at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges ..."). At most three words of credential. (writer; judge)
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out unless widely known; say what it does. (writer; judge)
- Full names, never a first name alone ("CEO Rahul"). (writer; judge)
- The line is a full sentence with its own subject, never "Recommends ...". (code: fragment, holds)
- Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans". Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models".
- Bad: "GenRobot to present human-data systems at CoRL Research Night" / "Event page says GenRobot will present ...". Good: "GenRobot will show its human-data capture systems at CoRL" / "The robot data vendor says the systems record people's movements to train embodied AI."
- Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API". Good: one headline per story.

**Open with what happened, not who said it.** Credit once, naturally: a possessive ("in Airbnb's tests"), the maker as
the subject ("Moonshot AI released"), or a short ending ("Snorkel AI finds"). Never "X says" in both the headline and
the line. (code: credit_first, credit_twice; judge)

**The line adds what the headline leaves out.** The comparison, the scale, the catch, or who it affects, as the source
states it. It never restates the headline and never leans on it with "That is..." or "The aim is...". At most 24 words.
(code: repeats_headline holds the story, idea_length; judge)
- Headline: "Reflection AI cuts its model's needless refusals almost in half"
- Line: "Handshake, the career network behind Handshake AI, says it helped design the tests, and refusals of valid requests fell 3.1%."

**Few numbers, each with its meaning.** At most two key numbers across the headline and line; round to the meaning up
front ("almost in half") and keep the exact figure in the bullets. Never a number before what it measures; never
"percentage points" (write before and after). (code: too_many_numbers, percentage_points; judge)

**Plain words, field terms.** RL, SFT, eval, benchmark, rollout and LLM judge are fine. A paper's own acronyms, metric
names and method names are described in plain words or left out ("42% less compute", not "42.0% fewer total FLOPs").
(writer; judge)

**People get a short credential.** Two or three words from their verified role, before the name (or in the line when the headline would get long): "Illinois professor
Talia Ringer", "NVIDIA post-training lead Oleksii Kuchaiev". Never a credential the role does not state. (code:
person_label; judge)

**Lesser-known companies get a short descriptor** on first mention, 2 to 6 words, from their Directory line or what the
source says: "data vendor Julius AI". Never a guess: a company neither source nor Directory describes stays bare.
Well-known companies are named bare. (code: company_label; judge)

**Research papers say where the authors work.** Name the authors' companies or universities, as the paper's affiliation lines give them, in the headline, the first sentence or the summary's opening: "A Meta and NYU paper ...". Never an affiliation the paper does not show. (code: affiliation; writer; audit)

**Relay accounts are never the credit.** An account that only posts other people's papers or news (DailyPapers,
AK, digests) is not the maker; credit the authors or the organization. (code: relay_credit holds the story)

**Variety.** Headlines should not read like a template. Mix shapes: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a
person with their credential, a number. (code: same_opening for generic openings; the headline editor sees the last
12 headlines; judge)

**Straight headlines on the site.** No puns or pop-culture jokes on the site: its headlines are read alone in search,
RSS and share previews. Vivid verbs give it life ("catches", "halves", "stops saying no").

**Legal stories** say "alleges", "sued over" or "reportedly" and name the outlet. Never a joke about a lawsuit, a
layoff or a named person's misfortune. (code: allegation words; writer)

## 3. Bullets

Each bullet is evidence for the line or one new fact: the numbers with their baseline, the method, who is involved, the
catch. None repeats the headline or the line. At most 22 words each. (writer; judge)
